newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain experts eye grain quality after damp weather.
newsitem.headline: Spain experts eye grain quality after damp weather.

text.p: Rain and hail in two provinces in Spain's main cereal-producing area Castille-Leon could reduce the harvest, but the real threat to this year's crop is sustained damp weather, agricultural experts said on Thursday.
Hailstones and heavy rain fell in isolated areas in Vallodolid and Palencia on Wednesday causing flooding but overall limited damage, farmers' association ASAJA told Reuters.
But this was not what was worrying traders.
"The problem is not the quantity but the quality (of the crop) this year. Damage has been caused by the continual rain we've had," said a trader in the north who requested anonymity.
Spain has suffered unseasonably cool and wet weather since May. This month so far is the nation's most unstable July for the past twenty years, according to the national meteorological office.
Temperatures are forecast to fall again in the north this weekend, with more light rain possible.

"This latest storm may have damaged some isolated areas, but it's not something that's going to bring the tonnage down. It might affect an area of 50,000 hectares at the very most and some of that will be fruit as well as cereals," the trader added.

Castille-Leon produced around 2.1 million tonnes of soft wheat and about 4.6 million tonnes of barley in 1996. These figures are expected to fall to 1.5 million and 3.0 million tonnes respectively this year, official data show.
This is part of a total 1997 national forecast of 12.76 million tonnes of wheat and barley.
A spokeswoman for ASAJA in Palencia said experts were still assessing the situation, but in the two provinces she estimated the storm may have affected about 60 percent of total plantings.
To date the overall condition of barley and wheat looked likely to mean more imports, a Madrid trader said.

"The problem is quality. When the rain falls, (wheat and barley) crops germinate and that means they're no good for flour or malt. It will damage milling wheat, but then they can use that for feed wheat," he said.
"What will happen is that we'll have to import German and French crops to plug the (milling wheat) gap, but France is seeing the same problems as us," he added.
The northcentral region is on alert for possible further storms, and the local area has been declared a disaster zone, the Civil Guard told Reuters on Wednesday.
Rivers overflowed and flooded fields, damaging barley, wheat, oats, sugar beet and fruit in Palencia and Vallodolid, ASAJA said.
The group's Vallodolid spokesman said prices should start to fall as farmers are forced to sell crops of poor quality.
Some farmers have been hoarding stocks in an attempt to shore up prices, traders say.

But pressuring prices up is the fact that poor weather continues to delay harvesting, and ASAJA estimates that only one third of the barley crop has been collected so far, with wheat barely starting to be collected.
